Chapter 7: Overcoming Bias and Building Fairness.
Let’s be honest—no one’s completely immune to bias. Social psychology tells us that every single person carries unconscious preferences and stereotypes, shaped by our culture, upbringing, even the media we consume.
The tricky part? These biases can sneak into our decisions and shape how we interact with others, often without us even realizing it.
Think of biases as mental shortcuts. Our brains are wired to quickly make sense of a complicated world, so sometimes we rely on snap judgments. Sure, that can be helpful when we need to make quick decisions. But it can also lead to unfair outcomes and missed chances to truly connect with people.
For example, have you ever found yourself gravitating toward someone who just seems familiar, or making a split-second call about a stranger’s abilities? That’s bias in action—even if we don’t mean any harm.
Here’s something to pay attention to: The very first step in overcoming bias is simply being aware of it. Social psychology recommends a gentle, nonjudgmental approach here. Instead of feeling guilty that biases exist, notice them. Understand that they’re natural, but not set in stone. This kind of self-awareness can really open the door to change.
So, how do you start reducing bias in everyday life? Here are a few practical ideas:
Try seeking out diverse perspectives—not just through conversations, but also by reading different books, watching films from other cultures, or exploring viewpoints in the media.
When you’re making decisions where bias might sneak in—like hiring someone, evaluating a teammate, or settling a conflict—slow down. Give yourself time to think things through instead of relying only on gut feelings.
You can also use structured checklists or clear criteria to guide important choices. This helps keep those unconscious preferences in check.
Building fairness is an ongoing journey. It means questioning our assumptions, inviting honest feedback, and being willing to adjust as we learn. In group settings, fairness grows when everyone gets a chance to speak up, and when decisions are made out in the open.
So, here’s the key takeaway—by working to recognize and reduce our own biases, we help create spaces where more people feel truly seen, valued, and included.
